Convert a map into a hexagon tile map

Source: R/hexmap.R
hexmap.Rd

Replaces each region of a map with a hexagon of equal size. The hexagons tile the outline of the map, and each region is allocated the hexagon that minimises the total squared displacement of all regions.

Usage

hexmap(
  object,
  group = NULL,
  group_layout = layout_hierarchy(),
  island_gap = 0.5,
  group_gap = 0.1,
  crs = NULL
)

Arguments

object

An sf object, or a geometry column (sfc), of regions in a projected or longitude/latitude coordinate reference system.

group

Optionally, the group of each region (e.g. states), as a column of object given unquoted (group = state) or as a string (group = "state"), or as a vector with one value for each region.

group_layout

How groups are arranged, as a layout function such as layout_hierarchy() (the default), layout_diffusion(), layout_compact() or layout_slice(), optionally wrapped in layout_repair() to fix which groups touch. Only used with group.

island_gap

The distance, in hexagon widths, beyond which landmasses are tiled as separate islands. Use Inf to tile all land together.

group_gap

The width of the gap between groups, as a fraction of the hexagon width. The hexagons along group borders are trimmed to make this gap, so they are slightly smaller than other hexagons. Only used with group.

crs

The projected coordinate reference system to make the hexagons in, such as the one the map will be plotted in. object is transformed to crs with sf::st_transform(). Defaults to the CRS of object, or for longitude/latitude input, to a Lambert azimuthal equal-area CRS centred on the data ("+proj=laea +lat_0=... +lon_0=...").

Value

For an sf object, object with its geometry replaced by hexagons, keeping all of its other columns and the order of its rows, so the hexagons can be joined to or compared with the original regions. For a geometry column, a geometry column of hexagons in the same order, so hexmap() can be used within dplyr::mutate() to add the hexagons as another geometry column. The hexagons are in the coordinate reference system they were made in.

Details

Landmasses that are further apart than island_gap hexagon widths are tiled separately, with one hexagon for each region on that landmass. Their hexagons are separated by at least one empty hexagon, so islands such as Tasmania remain distinct from the mainland.

When group is given, the hexagons of each group (e.g. state) are kept contiguous and a gap of group_gap hexagon widths is cut along the borders between groups, so that each group is visually distinct. Groups usually need a very different area of hexagons than they cover on the map, so the map is distorted to fit them, as chosen by group_layout. By default, the groups are laid out first, keeping each group's shape and touching the groups it borders on the map, and the regions are then placed within each group. See layouts for the available layouts, and vignette("layouts") for how they compare. Grouping works best for groups that are spatially contiguous, such as states.

The hexagons are regular and equally sized in the coordinate reference system (CRS) they are made in, which is the CRS of object unless crs is given, or a Lambert azimuthal equal-area CRS centred on the data for longitude/latitude input. The hexagons keep their location when plotted in another projection, but are stretched by it, so make the hexagons in the CRS you will plot in. Use an equal-area CRS for hexagons that also cover equal areas on the ground. See vignette("projections") for details.

See also

hex_grid() and hex_allocate(), which make an ungrouped hexagon map in two steps: hexmap(x) is the same as hex_allocate(x, hex_grid(x)).

Examples

library(sf)
# The 2025 Australian federal election, in the Australian Albers projection
election <- st_transform(aus_election_2025, 3577)
# A hexagon for each electoral division
election_hex <- hexmap(election)

# Every column of the map is kept, in the same order
head(election_hex)
#> Simple feature collection with 6 features and 3 fields
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -1118770 ymin: -3831910 xmax: 1677985 ymax: -2287407
#> Projected CRS: GDA94 / Australian Albers
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   division state party                                                  geometry
#>   <chr>    <chr> <chr>                                             <POLYGON [m]>
#> 1 Adelaide SA    ALP   ((-875573.9 -2568225, -997171.9 -2498021, -997171.9 -235…
#> 2 Aston    VIC   ALP   ((340406.7 -3410682, 218808.6 -3340477, 218808.6 -320006…
#> 3 Ballarat VIC   ALP   ((-997171.9 -3200068, -1118770 -3129863, -1118770 -29894…
#> 4 Banks    NSW   ALP   ((1313191 -3831910, 1191593 -3761705, 1191593 -3621296, …
#> 5 Barker   SA    LP    ((-753975.8 -2778840, -875573.9 -2708635, -875573.9 -256…
#> 6 Barton   NSW   ALP   ((1556387 -3831910, 1434789 -3761705, 1434789 -3621296, …

# \donttest{
# Keep the divisions of each state together (takes a few seconds)
election_hex <- hexmap(election, group = state)
# }

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(election_hex) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = party))


# \donttest{
# Hexagons made for a globe centred on Australia
globe <- "+proj=ortho +lat_0=-25 +lon_0=134"
ggplot(hexmap(election, group = state, crs = globe)) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = state)) +
  coord_sf(crs = globe)

# }
# \donttest{
# Add the hexagons as a second geometry column, alongside the regions
election <- dplyr::mutate(election, hex = hexmap(geometry, group = state))
# }
